newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian poll candidates hold final rallies.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian poll candidates hold final rallies.

text.p: Thousands of Bulgarians braved cold and rain on Friday evening for the closing rallies of the two main candidates for Sunday's presidential election.
Opposition supporters gathered outside Sofia's ornate orthodox cathedral, traditional site for rallies of the anti-communist Union of Democratic Forces, to cheer lawyer Petar Stoyanov.
Across town, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov gathered a mostly elderly crowd of Socialist supporters outside the National Palace of Culture.
Some 6.75 million Bulgarians will be eligible to vote in their second presidential election since the fall of communism in 1989.

Since then, they have seen living standards fall steadily as Bulgaria slips ever further behind its ex Warsaw Pact neighbours and many political analysts expect a low turnout in protest at the lack of economic progress.
But the prospect of bread queues and fuel shortages this winter did not dull the candidates' rhetoric.
"Bulgaria is once again choosing its destiny," Stoyanov told the crowd, some of whom had Bulgarian flags tied to their umbrellas.

"Those countries which resolved their problems with a sense of national responsibility and not with nostalgia for communist ideology...have no bread queues and three meals a day are not a problem for them."
The president is a largely ceremonial figure with little power to influence the economic crisis but the outcome of the election may prove crucial for Prime Minister Zhan Videnov.
"We have achieved positive results already. The obvious proof that the country is benefiting from our reform is your smiling faces tonight," Videnov told the crowd.
Stoyanov has said a big opposition win would represent a vote of no confidence in the Socialists and has raised the possibility of early elections.

An opinion poll released by the Laboratory for Political Behaviour on Thursday showed 32.5 percent support for Stoyanov, 21.5 percent for Marazov, with maverick politician George Ganchev close behind on 18.5 percent.
Another 16 percent of the 1,570 people polled had not yet decided how they will vote.

"If Ganchev goes through to a second round he may very possibly win," political analyst Miroslav Sevlievski told Reuters. He said if Marazov was eliminated, many Socialist supporters would transfer their votes to Ganchev rather than vote for the candidate of the united opposition.
If the second round is between Stoyanov and Marazov, then the votes of Ganchev's supporters will be key.
Ganchev and his Bulgarian Business Bloc have traditionally attracted protest votes from people disillusioned with the two main parties.

Thirteen pairs of presidential and vice-presidential candidates are contesting Sunday's poll. If no one wins more than 50 percent in the first round, or turnout is less than 50 percent of the electorate, a second round will be held a week later.
